Through the window she could see bare pasture, the river, more grey stone, and beyond it nothing at all.

Vane walked her through the house that first day as a man reads a ledger. Here the library. Here the long gallery, where portraits of his ancestors stared past her—they had all married for land. Here the chapel, the servants' stairs, the small rooms. "Your rooms," he said, and corrected himself: "Our rooms." Then he went to his study, and she did not see him again until supper.

At supper he ate in silence, reading letters she was not invited to see. When he spoke, it was to give orders to the servants in her presence, as though she were a piece of furniture that happened to be sitting at the table. She would take supper at eight. She would attend service on Sundays. She would rest in the afternoon, because a lady in her condition must be kept in good order. He said this with a glance at her waist, and she understood what condition he meant.

He came to her chamber twice in the first month. It was a duty performed without warmth, like a man watering a field he means to plant. She lay still beneath him and thought of the north road—the height of the hedges, the name of the river. Afterward he slept, and she watched the dark shift beyond the window until the grey came back.

Martha became her keeper. She dressed Elara's hair, turned down her bed, followed her from room to room with soft, firm hands. She never raised her voice. She was the shape of everyday cruelty—the pause a moment too long at the door, the way her mouth pressed thin when Elara asked for paper, the way she said, "The baron likes a straight line," as if Elara were a plant to be staked. Elara learned to perform for her: to stand straight, to speak composedly, while inside she was a house whose windows had been boarded over.

She wandered. She walked the corridors in the afternoons, counting windows, memorizing the turn of stairways, mapping the fortress the way she had once mapped the road to Marstead—a gift for maps wasted in a house where every door led only to another room. The servants did not speak unless spoken to. She asked once, lightly, whether letters arrived with the post. The steward bowed and said, "Nothing for you, my lady." She was not certain he was lying. She was not certain he was telling the truth. That was the particular genius of the place: it made certainty impossible.

The library was vast, all leather and gilding, the collected works of dead men who had never known her. She read through it the way prisoners pace a cell. Words fell from the pages like dry seeds and took no root. She tried the poets, then the philosophers, then a volume of sermons, then a book on the management of cattle. The words tasted like ashes, soot in the mouth, and she put the books back on their shelves and did not remember what she had read.

Only her mother's thin book of poems she kept by the bed. She could not open it. When finally she did, one evening, the poem she had read to Callum by candlelight sat on the page like a small stone. She laid her hand over it and pressed until the paper creased, and then she shut the book and did not open it again for a long time.

The letters came with the carriers and drovers who passed the fortress on the road north. Callum wrote on whatever he could find—margins, old ledgers, the blank side of a broadsheet—and gave each folded page to a stranger, with the name of the house and the color of her hair. The steward had standing orders: anything not sealed with a house of standing went to the baron's study, unopened. Vane read each one by the fire, his face unreadable, and dropped it onto the coals. The paper curled, blackened, and was gone before supper. He did not tell Elara that letters had come. He did not forbid the mail. He simply made it ash.

In the evenings, after supper, Elara went to the window in her chamber and faced south. The road was out there somewhere, four days' walk from the old house to Marstead, except that there was no road for her anymore. She told herself the distance was long. He had been given nothing—no coin, no coat, a torn shirt and wounds the rain would find. It would take time to heal. Time to find paper. Time to trust a stranger with a name. She told herself no news was not the same as bad news. She had heard that somewhere, or invented it, and she held it like a stone in her pocket, wearing it smooth.

But the weeks turned over like the pages of a book she had already read. The study fire burned each evening at the same hour. Martha said, "Who would write to you? The house is paid for. The husband is got." Elara had no answer. She stopped asking.

She waited. The waiting became a room she lived in, a shape grown around her, invisible walls. She stood at the window and watched the river run past, slate-colored and indifferent, and thought of the sea she had never seen, the sea Callum had promised was kind. She had stopped hoping, if hope was the word for it. She waited not for a letter now but for something to change, for the days to carry her somewhere she did not have to choose.

She was not yet ash. She was paper, curling at the edges, held over a flame that had not quite touched her—waiting for a word that never came. The fire in the study burned on, and the river ran south, and the north road went on without her, and somewhere on it a man she had loved was walking, and she had no way to know.

chapters.name: The Wanderer
chapters.content:
The rain found his back before the scars had finished with it. For a week he walked with his shirt off when the weather let him, letting the sun and wind harden the wounds, and for a month after that he wore the shirt like a hair shirt, feeling each stitch catch on new skin. By the first frost the flogging was a map on him—white and purple, tugging at his shoulders whenever he reached for anything above his head. He did not reach much.

He was not yet thirty and looked twice it. He worked where work was offered: mucked stalls, hauled timber, bullied stones out of frozen fields for a penny a day. Hunger and walking had laid the flesh back over his ribs as lean rope, and men hired him for his back. But his hands were no longer his own. The ropes that had held him to the post through the dark had bitten through something in his wrists; his fingers shook when he tried to grip, and cramp seized them halfway through any fine work. He stood one morning at the door of a smithy and watched a man shoe a mare, the hammer coming down true again and again. Callum's hands remembered the weight. They would not hold it steady. The smith glanced at him once—at the hands—and did not offer him work. He turned and walked on, and that night he did not drink with the other hired men, because he did not want to explain.

The first letter took him three days. He found the paper in a peddler's abandoned pack, clean on one side, and bought a stub of pencil with the last pennies of a day's pay. He wrote in a cow byre by lantern light. His hand shook; the lines came out broken and heavy, and twice the cramp seized him and he had to press his wrists against his knees until they loosened.

"Elara," he wrote. "I told you I was all right and it was a lie. I am not all right. I am walking. I think of you every day, which is not a comfort. It is the only thing I have left. My hands are ruined; I cannot be the farrier I was going to be. I am sorry for the coin they took and the satchel and the book. If there is a way to you I have not found it yet, but I have not stopped looking. Do not marry him. Wait for me. I know that is a great deal to ask when I have nothing but this paper. Still. Wait for me."

He read it over and the words seemed small, no better than a mule's scrap of all he meant. He folded it along the creases of his palm and wrote on the outside: For the Lady Elara, dark-haired, at the grey fortress above the river. He gave it to a drover heading north with cattle.

"Get it to her," Callum said.

The drover looked at the paper, at Callum's wrists, at his face. "I'll try," he said. Men always said they would try. Callum watched until the cattle swallowed him out of sight.

The letter reached the fortress, folded and travel-stained, and the steward's standing orders were clear: anything not sealed with a house of standing went to the baron's study, unopened. Lord Vane opened it that night by the fire. He read the trembling lines once, holding the page to the light, and at the line about waiting he smiled a little, the way a man smiles at a child's drawing. It was an accounting matter already settled—a debt closed with one flogging. A wandering man's words cost nothing at all. He dropped the letter on the coals. The paper curled, blackened at the edges, flared yellow, and was gone. By morning the ash would be swept out with the rest.

Callum did not know. He wrote again a fortnight later, on the back of a broadsheet he had pulled from a market cross and smoothed. This one was shorter. "I have not stopped looking. If the letters do not reach you, it is not because I stopped writing. I saw the sea last week, from a hill above a harbor, and it was the grey thing I told you of, breathing. I had no one to say that to but you. I still have no one. Yours, Callum." He gave that one to a tinker woman walking the north road, and gave her a penny besides, because the road was long and he could not make it shorter. "If she reads it, she'll want you," the tinker woman said, kindly. He thanked her, because he had no other thing to say. The tinker woman kept her penny and her word as far as the fortress gate; the steward followed his orders, and that letter burned on the same fire a week later, read first, then fed to the coals.

The frosts came on. Work grew scarcer. He slept in barns and lime kilns and, once, in a church porch. He asked every traveler going north whether they had heard word of the lady at the grey fortress. They shook their heads. He told himself the letters had miscarried, or been thrown down, or been burned by Martha out of spite. No news was not the same as bad news, he told himself. But the silence sat in him like a stone in his boot, and walking on it wore his hope thin.

One night, over a fire of hedge clippings, he held a blank sheet of paper to the light and thought: she has not answered. She cannot answer, or she will not. He could not say which was worse. He almost put the paper in the fire; the flame touched a corner and he snatched it back and beat the spark out with his palm, smelling his own burned skin. He could no more stop writing to her than stop his breath. It was not hope anymore—not the bright thing it had been in the library. It was a habit of the heart, and habits outlive hope.

He wrote the last letter of the winter on a page torn from an old ledger, in ink he had traded a day's work for. His hand was steadier now, or the cold had numbed it. "I am coming north," he wrote, though he had no coin, no plan, and only his ruined hands. "I am coming north, and if you are not there I will keep walking until I am. Do not wait for me if it will cost you. But if you can—wait." He folded it small and gave it to the drover Lowick, who had shared his fire. "The grey fortress above the river," Callum said. "She has dark hair. She reads by the window." Lowick tied the letter inside his coat. "I'll see it handed over," he said, "or I'll burn it myself." Callum thought of the fire in the baron's study and swallowed. "Burn it, then," he said, "rather than let it be wasted." Lowick nodded. Callum watched him ride out at first light, the letter going north away from him, and then he picked up the empty sack that was all he owned and set his face north as well. He thought of asking Lowick to wait, to take another, better letter, but he had put everything he knew into the one folded page, and there was nothing better in him.

The rain began before noon—a cold, driving rain that found the old scars on his back and the new calluses on his hands and the place in his chest where his hope had been. He walked into it because there was nothing else to do, and because somewhere ahead a letter was going north to a woman who had never answered one, and because the pencil stub in his pocket was still sharp enough to write another. He felt for it with his thumb as he walked. It was there. That, somehow, was enough to keep him going.

chapters.name: The Ashes of Hope
chapters.content:
The years at the fortress did not pass so much as accumulate, like dust on a sill no one remembered to wipe.

She rose when the bell rang and dressed in what Martha laid out. She went down and ate what was put before her. She attended chapel on Sundays and sat through sermons she no longer felt. At supper she sat across from Lord Vane and spoke when spoken to, which was seldom. He entertained once or twice a season; she stood at his side in silk and said little, and the guests learned not to address her. These were the duties of her station, and she performed them the way a clock performs the hour: the hands moved, the bell sounded, no one was changed by it.

For a year the baron had come to her room as a man waters a field he means to plant. When the field gave nothing, he stopped. He did not rage; he wasted nothing on her, not even contempt. She had failed her single purpose and so was kept the way failed things are kept—on a shelf, out of the way, until someone remembers to throw them out. He spoke of her once while going over the household accounts—a list of cattle and a lady—and she understood she was an inventory item that had not bred. Martha had grown sleek on the same understanding; her cruelty was smoother now, a matter of pauses and small refusals. "The baron likes a straight line," she said when Elara asked for paper, as if Elara were a hem to be measured. Elara stopped asking.

Her days contracted around that. She read through the library in the long afternoons—sermons, histories, a treatise on oak. The words went in and out of her like light through a cracked window, leaving nothing on the floor. Her mother's book stayed by her bed, but she did not open it. The poem she had read to Callum lay inside it like a pressed flower, and she could not bear to touch the page where it sat creased.

The south window faced the river. Once she had watched it from that window, telling herself the distance was long, that no news was not the same as bad news. She had once wanted to see the sea; the wanting was gone the way money goes—she could remember having it, but not what it had felt like in her hand. When at last she understood that no word would come—that whatever had happened to him on the north road had happened, and she would never know it—she stopped watching. The window became only a window. The river became only water, going somewhere else.

Callum walked north through the winter and into the country of the grey fortress, though he never went near the fortress itself. He worked where work offered—mucking stalls, hauling timber, pulling stones from frozen fields—rough work that asked nothing of his ruined hands. The hands shook at fine work; they could not hold a hammer steady, so he did not hold a hammer. Men hired him for his back and his silence, and he gave them both.

He was not yet thirty-two and looked fifty. The flogging had mapped itself across his shoulders in white and purple, and the scars tugged at him in cold weather. He slept in barns and outbuildings and once, in a hard month, in a church porch. He moved from town to town, staying where there was work and leaving when it ended. He had no fixed address; he was a man the world passed through. Only horses remembered him—they stood quiet when he came near, and a farmer paid him once for calming a mare that had kicked two men. He took the coin and walked on. He no longer asked travelers for word of the lady at the grey fortress. There had been a drover who said, "She'll be that one now—the baron's lady," as if that settled everything, and Callum had felt it settle in him too, a stone dropping in a well.

He wrote to Elara still. Paper, pencil, ink traded for a day's work. He gave the letters to travelers going north—a drover, a tinker, a peddler of ribbons—and asked each to deliver them to the lady at the grey fortress above the river. He no longer expected an answer. He wrote the way other men pray, to a silence that might or might not listen. It was not hope anymore but a habit of the heart, and habits outlive hope. The letters went north, season after season, and the silence came back to him empty—and he wrote again anyway, because the writing was the only place he still existed whole.

The letters reached the fortress. The steward's standing orders directed anything unsealed by a house of standing to the baron's study, unopened. In the first years Vane read them by the fire, smiling at the handwriting, at the man who did not know when he was beaten. But they kept coming—winter, spring, another winter—until reading them grew wearisome. "Burn them," he said at last, and the steward obeyed. After that the envelopes were carried straight to the fireplace, a season's worth at a time, unopened, and fed to the coals. The drover Lowick's letter, handed faithfully over at the gate, burned with the rest. No one read it.

On an afternoon of thin rain, Elara crossed the inner hall on an errand she had forgotten by the time she reached the far door. A servant passed her carrying a stack of envelopes toward the study fireplace—plain paper, none of the house's seals. The addresses were written in a hand that had been sure once and had since learned to fit the page the way a man writes left-handed.

She saw them. For a moment the sight pressed against something old in her chest, a muscle that remembered being used. It failed her. The question of who wrote, and why, had been starved so long inside her that it could not lift its head. The servant did not pause. The envelopes shifted in his arms. There was a fire waiting for them, and a stack of paper to feed it. She looked away before she could read a single name.

She let him pass. She did not hear the study door close, or the first envelope taken up, or the ink curling and blackening as the flames rose and the words she had waited for all those years rose with them, once, and then were gone.

She had forgotten to wonder. It was the same as never knowing.

That evening a maid swept the study hearth and carried the ashes out in a bucket, and the thin rain fell on them. It did not matter. The last embers of Elara's hope had died unseen, and no one—not even she—had watched them go.

chapters.name: The Market Fair
chapters.content:
The fair had taken the river meadows below the town, and for one day the world was all noise and color. Booths of striped canvas stood in rows; a piper played against a tinker hammering tin. Pennants snapped in the wind. Elara walked a half-step behind Lord Vane, as she had for so many years she no longer noticed the position. Her skirt of dove-grey silk hissed over the trodden grass. Two footmen and Martha came behind her. The sunlight was painful; she had grown used to the dim of the fortress.

Vane was in a good humor, which meant he was spending. He had bought a mare at the horse lines and now moved along the edge of the fair with the air of a man finishing the year's business. "Keep close," he said without turning. "There are thieves among crowds."

Elara kept close. She watched the stalls pass—cheese, cloth, a man with caged songbirds—and found that none of it reached her. She was a window with the shutters drawn. Even the sunlight went through her. She had learned to stand still in her cage until the cage was carried somewhere else; this was only a larger cage with pennants.

Ahead, at the far edge of the horse lines, a small crowd had gathered. Vane moved toward it, because he was a man who owned horses and wanted to see foolishness in other people's. Elara followed.

The object of the crowd was a pony. It was a ruined animal—old, swaybacked, ribs standing along its sides, a coat of scars and rain rash. It stood with its head low and its eyes half closed, the way animals do when they have been beaten past caring. The man holding its lead rope was more ruinous still. His clothes were good once and had been worn years too long; the line of his back under the worn coat was a line that remembered bearing weight. His hands were the hands of a man who had been broken and never set right: the fingers crooked, the knuckles misaligned. He held the rope in a fist the way men hold tools they no longer trust.

A dealer was shaking his head. "Not worth a shilling," he said. "Knacker's price and nothing more."

The man with the pony said nothing. He stood still, and the pony stood still with him, quiet in a way that was not the quiet of defeat. The dealer prodded at the pony's mouth. The pony did not move.

Elara looked away. She had learned to look away from suffering; the fortress had taught her thoroughly.

But something in the angle of the man's shoulders was familiar. Something in the way he waited. She looked again. He turned then, or lifted his head as if her looking had touched him, and she saw his face.

The crowd sounds fell away.

She saw the ruin of the man she had loved. The face was weathered beyond its years—the man was not yet thirty-two and looked fifty—with deep lines cut by weather and want. The brown hair was greying at the temples. The eyes, when they found hers, were the same eyes. She had forgotten they were the same.

The pony stood quietly at the end of its rope. Callum did not move. He looked at her across the trampled grass, and she looked at him, and the only sound in the world was the fair going on without them.

She saw in his face every north-road mile, every winter he had walked, the flogging's residue in the way he held himself slightly turned, as if protecting his back from the sun. She saw the hands that would never hold a farrier's hammer again, the fingers that could not do fine work. She saw that he was poor, and that the poverty had gone into him like rain into wood.

And even ruined, he was the same. The thing she had loved was still there—the steadiness, the quiet. The pony stood quiet for him, the way horses had always stood quiet for him, and that was the worst of it, because she saw he was still the man who had promised to find a way.

She wanted to speak. The words rose in her—his name, a word, anything—and died in the crushing silence. Behind her, Martha's voice, careful and thin: "My lady. You're staring."

Elara did not move.

And across the trampled grass, Callum read her face exactly backward, the way a man reads the sky for weather and names the storm that will never come.

He saw the silks. He saw the jewels at her throat, the guarded blankness of a woman who has learned to stand still. He saw Lord Vane at her shoulder, broad and iron-haired, and the two footmen, and Martha, sleek in her duty. He saw a woman of another world, a world he had touched once by candlelight in a moldering library, and the gulf was not the gulf of miles but of everything that had happened since. She had married the baron. She had been taken to the grey fortress. She had worn the silk until the silk became her.

The letters rose in him—all the letters he had written and given to drovers, tinkers, peddlers of ribbons, pouring his heart onto paper like a man filling a grave. She had never answered. She had never tried. He had told himself for years that the letters were lost, unread, burned. But seeing her now, in her silks, walking a half-step behind her husband, he believed he understood at last: she had chosen her cage. Or she had been broken into it until choosing and being broken were the same, and either way she was not his. He would not be the man who called a lady's name across a fair.

He turned. He did not look back. He walked away from the pony, from the dealer shouting after him, from the price he had needed and no longer cared about. The crowd took him. He went into it like a stone into water and was gone.

Elara watched the place where he had been. The crowd closed over it. She stood very still, the way she had stood at her father's table and at the altar and in the baron's bed, and something inside her broke quietly, without sound, the way a muscle gives way. She had not known there was anything left to break. She had told herself for years that her hope was dead—that she had forgotten to wonder—and yet there had been something down in her, deeper than thinking, a fragment that had waited. A fragment that had believed, without her permission, that he was still alive somewhere with the same eyes, the same quiet hands. That if she ever saw him again, the silence between them would fill with everything that had not been said.

She did not know he had written. She knew only that no word had reached her, and that he had seen her—the silks, the jewels, the baron's hand at her shoulder—and had turned away. He had looked at the woman she had become and had given up. That was the truth of it. There was no worse truth.

"Martha," said Lord Vane, without interest. "Her color is bad. Bring her to the carriage."

Elara let herself be led. She did not watch the crowd. She did not wonder where he was walking, what road he would take, whether he would eat that night. The fragment inside her, the last living part, had come apart when he turned, and now she was at peace. That was the terrible thing about the end of hope. It felt so much like peace.

chapters.name: The River
chapters.content:
The carriage climbed toward the fortress through sheets of rain. Vane sat across from her, unmoved by the sway of the wheels, his broad hands folded on the head of his walking stick. He had not spoken since the fair, and yet his silence had a texture, a weight, like the rain pressing against the glass. Once, years ago, she had heard him list her among the household accounts—cattle and a lady—and the memory returned now with the rhythm of the wheels. She was inventory. Inventory was returned to its place.

The great doors closed behind them with the sound of a tomb. Martha was waiting with a lamp. The light showed her thin face, the mouth pressed into the line the baron liked, the eyes that had counted every slight for years and fed on them until they were sleek. "My lady," she said, and nothing more. The silence was a full statement. *I saw you staring at the ruin at the horse lines. I saw your color come up. I will remember it.* Martha had bought her place with one betrayal; she had spent every year since making sure the price was still being paid.

The silks came off like a shed skin. Martha's hands were brisk, indifferent, professional. She did not speak until Elara stood in her shift, and then she said, "His lordship says you will not dine tonight. He says your color is still bad."

It was not a punishment. It was the nearest thing to attention Elara had received from Vane in a year, and she was not even worth that.

Martha turned down the lamp, a small cruelty administered gently, and left. The door closed—not locked, because she was not worth locking in. And then there was only the rain on the south window.

She stood at the window a long time, or a short time. She had lost the distinction between them somewhere between the flogging and the wedding, between the wedding and the year Vane stopped coming to her bed. He had visited her at first the way he did everything, as a matter of business, watering a field he meant to plant. When the field gave nothing, he had stopped without rage, and she had understood she was failed property, kept the way failed things were kept: out of the way, unremarked, unneeded.

The river was below, swollen and grey as slate, running toward the sea she had never seen. She had watched it in the first years, telling herself that no news was not the same as bad news. She had stopped watching the day she understood there would be no news. The wanting of the sea had died like money spent, but the river was still there, still grey, still breathing in the dark.

The memory of the fair burned through her without flame.

He had stood at the far edge of the horse lines with the ruined pony, more ruinous than the animal he held—clothes good once and worn years too long, hair grey at the temples, hands broken and never set right. Even ruined he had been quiet and steady; the pony stood quiet for him, and that had been the worst of it, because it meant he was still himself. She had opened her mouth to call his name. The word had died in her throat, buried under the silence of years, under every letter she had never received and every hope she had forgotten to have.

He had looked at her silks and jewels, at the guarded blankness of the woman she had become, and had read her face exactly backward—the way a man reads the sky for weather and names the storm that will never come. He had turned without a word and walked into the crowd, leaving behind the pony he had needed to sell, the price he had come for. No call, no crossing of the space between them. Just the turn of a back that would forever carry the flogging's map.

She had told herself at the fair that the fragment inside her had broken, and that she was at peace, and it had felt like peace. That was the terrible thing about the end of hope—how much it resembled rest. But standing at the south window in the dark, she understood the fragment was not broken. It was the shape of a man walking away. It would turn and turn, forever, in the chest of a woman standing at a window with rain on the glass.

The largest choices made themselves without deciding. She had learned that when the lanterns blazed in the stable yard, and again when the ivory silk was fitted, and every morning of every year she had woken in another woman's house and pulled back another woman's hair. You did not choose. The road chose you, and then you followed it.

She put her mother's book in the drawer and did not open it. The Marstead letter was gone, taken or burned; the poems were only poems. She dressed in the dark in clothes that were not her own—a plain gown, a worn cloak, shoes made for walking corridors, not paths. She took nothing. There was nothing left to take, and taking would have been a lie, a suggestion that she meant to go somewhere.

The servants' stairs were dark. She knew their turnings by heart, as she knew the chapel where vows had been said, the study where the steward fed unsealed letters to the coals, the gallery where her footsteps echoed like someone else's. At the foot of the stairs she passed the library door and did not stop. The words she had read there had gone through her like light through a cracked window. There was no comfort in them.

The rain met her at the side door.

It struck her face like a cold hand, and for one breath something old rose in her—the girl who had promised she would not be sold, who had put herself between Callum and the whip. That girl wanted to run. That girl still thought there was a way, that a drove-road could be walked in the dark, that a river could be followed to the sea he had seen.

But that girl was years gone. The flogging had taken her, the marriage had taken the rest, and the fair had taken what remained. There was nothing left of her to run.

The path was steep and slick with mud. She took it slowly, carefully, the way a woman takes her last walk with dignity. The river sound grew as she descended—a low, moving, breathing sound, the grey thing at the bottom of the dark. Rain filled her shoes. Mud pulled at her heels, once, twice, as if the path were trying to hold her back. It was only the path.

She reached the river without knowing she had reached it. The water was swollen, dark, running fast, no longer slate-colored but black, carrying the rain from all the hills it had passed before this one. It would carry her the same way, if she let it.

She stepped in.

The cold was a shock, a hand closing on her ankles. She kept walking. The water rose to her knees, her waist. Her cloak billowed on the current, dragging her, asking her to hurry. She did not hurry. She did not fight. The current found her and took her, gently, the way a man takes the hand of a woman who has given up dancing and leads her off the floor.

She was under. The cold stopped being cold, became a blankness, a silence, a letter laid down at last unread.

The last thought she had was not of her father, not of the broken house, not of the vows. It was of the fair, of his back vanishing into the crowd, of the word that had died in her throat and that she had let die there. It was of all the words she would never know were written to her and burned before she could read them. She believed to the last that they had never been worth fighting for—his hands, her hope, the sea, any of it—and the river agreed with her.

The river took her quietly. It did not struggle, and neither did she. She had never seen the sea, but below the river's grey, she thought she saw at last the grey thing he had spoken of, breathing, and it was waiting for her.
